question: Electrical Concepts - Resistance
stem: Which statement best describes the concept of electrical resistance in a circuit?
options: It is the pushing force that drives electric current through the wires.
It is a measure of how difficult it is for electric current to flow through a material.
It is the total number of battery cells connected in an electrical circuit.
It is the rate at which electrical energy is turned into chemical energy.
answer: It is a measure of how difficult it is for electric current to flow through a material.

question: Circuit Dynamics - Adding Batteries
stem: If an extra battery is added in series to a simple circuit with one bulb, what happens to the electrical push and current?
options: The electrical push increases, causing a greater flow of current through the bulb.
The electrical push decreases, causing the current in the circuit to drop to zero.
The electrical push stays the same because the bulb determines total current.
The electrical push increases, but the current decreases due to thicker wires.
answer: The electrical push increases, causing a greater flow of current through the bulb.

question: Circuit Dynamics - Series Changes
stem: Two identical bulbs are connected in series with two batteries. What happens to the brightness of both bulbs if one battery is removed?
options: Both bulbs will become noticeably dimmer.
One bulb goes out while the other remains bright.
Both bulbs will become noticeably brighter.
The brightness of both bulbs remains unchanged.
answer: Both bulbs will become noticeably dimmer.

question: Measuring Instruments - Voltmeter Connection
stem: A student mistakenly connects a voltmeter in series inside a single-bulb circuit. What will be observed?
options: The bulb lights up very brightly and the connecting wires melt.
The bulb does not light up because voltmeters allow almost no current to pass.
The battery explodes due to a complete short circuit across its terminals.
The voltmeter accurately measures the current flowing through the light bulb.
answer: The bulb does not light up because voltmeters allow almost no current to pass.

question: Measuring Instruments - Circuit Symbols
stem: Which circuit diagram symbol represents an instrument used to measure the rate of flow of electricity?
options: A circle containing the letter 'V'
A circle containing the letter 'A'
A rectangle with a diagonal line through it
A circle containing the letter 'M'
answer: A circle containing the letter 'A'

question: Circuit Analysis - Resistance Comparison
stem: Bulb X and Bulb Y are tested separately with the same battery. The ammeter reads 0.4 A for Bulb X and 0.9 A for Bulb Y. What can you conclude?
options: Bulb X has higher resistance than Bulb Y because less current flows through it.
Bulb Y has higher resistance than Bulb X because more current flows through it.
Both bulbs have identical resistance because the battery used is the same.
It is impossible to compare resistance without knowing the length of the connecting wires.
answer: Bulb X has higher resistance than Bulb Y because less current flows through it.

question: Circuit Fault Finding - Series Circuit
stem: A decorative string of 20 festive lamps is wired in a single series loop. Why is it tedious to locate a single faulty lamp when the string fails?
options: The remaining working lamps become too bright to look at safely.
All lamps go out simultaneously, so each lamp must be tested individually.
The parallel branches continue drawing large currents from the wall socket.
The fuse automatically disconnects every individual bulb socket permanently.
answer: All lamps go out simultaneously, so each lamp must be tested individually.

question: Circuit Operation - Parallel Switches
stem: In a home lighting circuit with lamps in parallel, what happens when the switch for the bedroom lamp is turned off?
options: Only the bedroom branch is disconnected; other lamps in different rooms stay lit.
All lamps throughout the entire home turn off because the main loop is broken.
The remaining lamps in other rooms become significantly dimmer.
The current flowing from the main supply increases dramatically.
answer: Only the bedroom branch is disconnected; other lamps in different rooms stay lit.

question: Circuit Advantages - Parallel Arrangement
stem: Why are major electrical appliances (e.g. ovens, refrigerators) wired in parallel across the household mains supply?
options: Each appliance receives the full mains electrical push and operates independently.
Connecting appliances in parallel ensures that the total household current remains near zero.
Parallel wiring forces all appliances to consume identical amounts of electrical power.
Series circuits are prohibited because they make appliances heat up too quickly.
answer: Each appliance receives the full mains electrical push and operates independently.

question: Parallel Circuits - Current Distribution
stem: A parallel circuit splits into two paths: Path A has a lower resistance than Path B. How does current divide between them?
options: Path A draws more current than Path B because electricity flows more easily through lower resistance.
Path B draws more current than Path A because higher resistance attracts more current.
Both paths draw exactly equal current because they share the same battery source.
All current travels along Path B while Path A receives no current at all.
answer: Path A draws more current than Path B because electricity flows more easily through lower resistance.

question: Unit Conversions - Power Ratings
stem: An electric toaster has a power rating of 800 W. What is its power rating expressed in kilowatts (kW)?
options: 8.0 kW
0.8 kW
answer: 0.8 kW

question: Cost Calculation - Power Conversion
stem: An LED floodlight is rated at 200 W. How much electrical energy in kWh does it consume if it remains on for 10 hours?
options: 20.0 kWh
2.0 kWh
0.2 kWh
2000 kWh
answer: 2.0 kWh

question: Cost Calculation - Time in Minutes
stem: A microwave oven rated at 1.2 kW is used to heat food for 30 minutes. How much electrical energy is consumed?
options: 36.0 kWh
0.6 kWh
2.4 kWh
0.04 kWh
answer: 0.6 kWh

question: Cost Calculation - Multi-step Problem
stem: An air conditioner rated at 2 kW runs for 5 hours each day. If electricity costs 25 cents per kWh, what is the daily running cost?

question: Cost Calculation - Appliance Comparison
stem: Appliance X (3 kW) is used for 2 hours, while Appliance Y (1 kW) is used for 8 hours. Which appliance consumes more energy?
options: Appliance X consumes more energy (6 kWh vs 8 kWh).
Appliance Y consumes more energy (8 kWh vs 6 kWh).
Both appliances consume the exact same amount of energy.
Appliance X consumes more energy because its power rating is higher.
answer: Appliance Y consumes more energy (8 kWh vs 6 kWh).

question: Electrical Safety - Frayed Cords
stem: Why does an electrical appliance cord with cracked outer plastic pose an immediate safety risk?
options: The exposed inner copper wire can be touched directly, resulting in an electric shock.
The electricity will continuously leak out into the room air, wasting electrical energy.
The appliance will draw twice as much voltage from the socket, burning out the motor.
The cracked plastic attracts moisture that causes the circuit breaker to rust.
answer: The exposed inner copper wire can be touched directly, resulting in an electric shock.

question: Dangers of Electricity - Wet Hands
stem: Why must electrical switches never be operated with wet hands?
options: Water is a good conductor that lowers skin resistance, allowing current to flow into the body.
Water causes the switch mechanism to produce a high magnetic field that damages nearby devices.
Water increases the voltage supplied by the mains socket beyond its normal limit.
Water cools down the switch contacts, preventing the circuit from closing properly.
answer: Water is a good conductor that lowers skin resistance, allowing current to flow into the body.

question: Electrical Safety - Circuit Breaker Tripping
stem: When several high-power appliances in a kitchen are switched on together, the master circuit breaker trips. Why does this happen?
options: The total current drawn exceeded the safe limit, triggering the breaker to cut power and prevent fire.
The appliances ran out of electrical energy and signalled the breaker to shut down.
The circuit breaker detected that one of the appliances was operating at too low a resistance.
The voltage supplied by the power station dropped to zero automatically.
answer: The total current drawn exceeded the safe limit, triggering the breaker to cut power and prevent fire.

question: Electrical Safety - Fuses vs Circuit Breakers
stem: What is an operational advantage of using a modern circuit breaker over a traditional fuse?
options: A circuit breaker can simply be reset with a switch, whereas a blown fuse wire must be replaced.
A circuit breaker completely eliminates the need for plastic insulation on wires.
A circuit breaker allows appliances to operate without consuming any electrical energy.
A circuit breaker increases the current capacity of all connected household cables.
answer: A circuit breaker can simply be reset with a switch, whereas a blown fuse wire must be replaced.

question: Materials - Poor Conductors in Safety
stem: Why are electrical plugs and cable sheaths manufactured using materials that are poor conductors of electricity?
options: They prevent electric current from passing to the outside surfaces where users make contact.
They allow electrical energy to move at much higher speeds through the internal wires.
They convert excess electrical current into light rather than releasing heat.
They increase the electrical push delivered to low-power household devices.
answer: They prevent electric current from passing to the outside surfaces where users make contact.

question: Dangers of Electricity - Adapter Overloading
stem: Plugging four high-power heating appliances into a single wall socket adapter causes the adapter cord to feel hot. What causes this heating?
options: The total current flowing through the adapter cable is excessively large, generating intense heat.
The wall socket is supplying too little push, forcing appliances to generate extra heat.
The plastic insulation around the adapter cord is absorbing electrical current.
The appliances are returning electrical energy back into the mains supply.
answer: The total current flowing through the adapter cable is excessively large, generating intense heat.

question: Dangers of Electricity - Damaged Insulation
stem: What is the primary danger if two bare, damaged wires inside an appliance cord touch each other while plugged in?
options: A short circuit is formed, causing a massive surge of current that can spark and start a fire.
The appliance stops working permanently because all electrical push is drained away.
The resistance of the circuit increases dramatically, slowing down the flow of electricity.
The power consumption of the appliance drops to zero while remaining on.
answer: A short circuit is formed, causing a massive surge of current that can spark and start a fire.

question: Electrical Safety - Undersized Fuses
stem: An electric kettle that requires 10 A of current is fitted with a 3 A fuse. What will happen when the kettle is switched on?
options: The fuse wire will melt immediately, breaking the circuit before the kettle can heat up.
The kettle will heat up normally but take three times as long to boil water.
The kettle body will become electrified and deliver an electric shock to the user.
The electrical cables inside the wall will instantly catch fire.
answer: The fuse wire will melt immediately, breaking the circuit before the kettle can heat up.

question: Dangers of Electricity - Mains Supply Hazards
stem: Why does mains electricity in homes (230 V) pose a much greater danger of severe electric shock than a standard 1.5 V dry cell?
options: The high push of mains electricity can drive dangerously large currents through the human body.
Mains electricity travels through metal wires, whereas dry cells do not use metal conductors.
Dry cells do not produce any electrical current when connected in complete circuits.
Mains electricity circuits cannot be fitted with safety fuses or circuit breakers.
answer: The high push of mains electricity can drive dangerously large currents through the human body.
